title: Diagonalisation and Powers
intro: If a matrix has enough eigenvectors, then in their directions it does nothing but stretch, and every hard question about it becomes easy. This page turns that idea into the factorisation $A = PDP^{-1}$, uses it to compute $A^{10}$ without multiplying ten times, and then finds the closed formula for the Fibonacci numbers.

blocks.text: Why change the axes

Look at $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ again. In the usual axes it turns most vectors, and applying it twice means a messy product. But we know two special directions, $v_1 = (1, 1)$ with $\lambda_1 = 5$ and $v_2 = (1, -2)$ with $\lambda_2 = 2$ (found on Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues)). Any vector can be written as a combination of them. Take $(3, 0)$. We want $c_1 (1, 1) + c_2 (1, -2) = (3, 0)$: the second entries give $c_1 = 2c_2$ and the first give $c_1 + c_2 = 3$, so $c_2 = 1$ and $c_1 = 2$, and $(3, 0) = 2\,v_1 + 1\,v_2$. Now apply $A$, using only that $A$ is linear and that $v_1, v_2$ are eigenvectors:

Check with the matrix: $A(3, 0) = (12, 6)$. It agrees. In the coordinates $(c_1, c_2)$ built on the eigenvectors, $A$ just multiplies the first by 5 and the second by 2, and nothing is mixed. Applying $A$ ten times multiplies them by $5^{10}$ and $2^{10}$. That is the entire idea of diagonalisation (US spelling: diagonalization); what remains is to write it as matrix algebra.
Building P and D
Put the eigenvectors side by side as the columns of a matrix $P$, and the eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of a matrix $D$:

Multiply $A$ by $P$. A matrix times a matrix works column by column: the first column of $AP$ is $A$ times the first column of $P$, and so on. So the columns of $AP$ are $Av_1$ and $Av_2$, which are $\lambda_1 v_1$ and $\lambda_2 v_2$:

blocks.tex: AP = \begin{pmatrix} Av_1 & Av_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 v_1 & \lambda_2 v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1 & v_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \end{pmatrix} = PD

blocks.text: The last step is also a column statement: $P$ times a diagonal matrix scales its first column by $\lambda_1$ and its second by $\lambda_2$. With the numbers, $AP$ has first column $A(1, 1) = (5, 5)$ and second column $A(1, -2) = (2, -4)$; and $PD$ has columns $5\,(1, 1) = (5, 5)$ and $2\,(1, -2) = (2, -4)$. Both are $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 5 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$. So $AP = PD$ holds. Because the eigenvectors are not parallel, $P$ is invertible (its determinant is $-2 - 1 = -3$), and multiplying on the right by $P^{-1}$ gives the factorisation

The inverse of a 2×2 matrix swaps the diagonal, negates the off-diagonal and divides by the determinant: $P^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{-3}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Check that it is the inverse: the top row of $P$ times the columns of $P^{-1}$ gives $\tfrac13(2 + 1) = 1$ and $\tfrac13(1 - 1) = 0$, and the bottom row gives $\tfrac13(2 - 2) = 0$ and $\tfrac13(1 + 2) = 1$. It is $I$. The full check of the factorisation is

Read $A = PDP^{-1}$ from right to left as a recipe: $P^{-1}$ turns ordinary coordinates into eigenvector coordinates (that is how the numbers $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = 1$ were found: $P^{-1}(3, 0) = (2, 1)$); $D$ stretches each coordinate; $P$ turns the result back into ordinary coordinates. The word for this is a change of basis.
Powers
Now square it. $A^2 = (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1}) = PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}$, because $P^{-1}P = I$ in the middle. The same cancellation happens at every join, so for every $k$
The power of a diagonal matrix is just the powers of its entries, with no multiplication of matrices at all. For our example:

Check $k = 1$: $\tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 3 \\ 6 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$, which is $A$. Check $k = 0$: $\tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = I$. Check $k = 2$ against the direct product $A \cdot A$: the top left is $4 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 = 18$, and the formula gives $\tfrac13(2 \cdot 25 + 4) = 18$. Good. Now $k = 10$, where $5^{10} = 9\,765\,625$ and $2^{10} = 1024$:

Look at the sizes. $5^{10}$ is nearly ten thousand times larger than $2^{10}$, so $A^{10}$ is almost entirely the $5^{10}$ part: every column is close to a multiple of $v_1 = (1, 1)$. Apply it to $(1, 0)$ and you get $(6\,510\,758,\ 6\,509\,734)$, whose entries differ by only 0.016 percent. After ten steps the vector has been pulled almost exactly onto the dominant eigen-direction. That is power iteration, taken up in Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration).

Example: the Fibonacci numbers

The Fibonacci numbers are $0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \ldots$, each the sum of the two before: $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. To put that in matrix form, keep the last two in a vector and ask what one step does:

The top row says $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$ and the bottom says $F_n = F_n$. Starting from $(F_1, F_0) = (1, 0)$, after $n$ steps the vector is $(F_{n+1}, F_n)$, so with $M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ we have $M^n = \begin{pmatrix} F_{n+1} & F_n \\ F_n & F_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}$. (Check $n = 2$: $M^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, with $F_3 = 2$, $F_2 = 1$, $F_1 = 1$.) To get a far-off Fibonacci number we need the power of $M$, so diagonalise it.
The trace is 1 and the determinant is $-1$, so the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 - \lambda - 1$. The roots are $\lambda = (1 \pm \sqrt{5})/2$:

These are the golden ratio $\varphi$ and its partner. Their sum is 1 (the trace) and their product is $-1$ (the determinant), so $\psi = -1/\varphi$. Each satisfies $\lambda^2 = \lambda + 1$. The shortcut $(b, \lambda - a)$ gives $(1, \lambda - 1)$ as an eigenvector, but a neater choice is $(\lambda, 1)$: check $M(\lambda, 1) = (\lambda + 1,\ \lambda) = (\lambda^2, \lambda) = \lambda\,(\lambda, 1)$, using $\lambda^2 = \lambda + 1$. So $v_1 = (\varphi, 1)$ and $v_2 = (\psi, 1)$.

Now write the starting vector $(1, 0)$ in the eigenvectors: $(1, 0) = c_1 (\varphi, 1) + c_2 (\psi, 1)$. The second entries give $c_1 + c_2 = 0$, so $c_2 = -c_1$; the first give $c_1(\varphi - \psi) = 1$ and $\varphi - \psi = \sqrt5$, so $c_1 = 1/\sqrt5$ and $c_2 = -1/\sqrt5$. Applying $M^n$ multiplies each part by its eigenvalue $n$ times:
The second entry is Binet's formula:

Check small cases. $n = 1$: $(\varphi - \psi)/\sqrt5 = \sqrt5/\sqrt5 = 1$. $n = 2$: $\varphi^2 - \psi^2 = (\varphi - \psi)(\varphi + \psi) = \sqrt5 \cdot 1$, so $F_2 = 1$. For larger $n$ use numbers. $n = 10$: $\varphi^{10} = 122.99187$ and $\psi^{10} = 0.00813$, so $F_{10} = (122.99187 - 0.00813)/2.236068 = 55$. For $n = 30$: $\varphi^{30} = 1\,860\,498.0$ (to one decimal), $\psi^{30} \approx 5.4 \times 10^{-7}$ and $F_{30} = 832\,040$, the true value.

Because $|\psi| < 1$, the term $\psi^n$ shrinks to nothing, and for $n = 20$ it is $0.00007$. So $F_n$ is simply the whole number nearest to $\varphi^n/\sqrt5$: for $n = 20$, $\varphi^{20}/\sqrt5 = 6765.00003$, and $F_{20} = 6765$. It also shows why the ratio of neighbours settles down: $F_{n+1}/F_n \to \varphi$, the dominant eigenvalue (that ratio is 1.6 at $n = 5$, 1.619 at $n = 8$ and 1.6182 at $n = 10$, since $F_6/F_5 = 8/5$, $F_9/F_8 = 34/21$, $F_{11}/F_{10} = 89/55$). It is power iteration again: the $\varphi$ part of the vector grows and the $\psi$ part dies.

When it works, and when it fails
The factorisation needs $n$ independent eigenvectors for an $n \times n$ matrix, so that $P$ has an inverse. A matrix with that property is diagonalisable. There are two cases to know.

Distinct eigenvalues guarantee it. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are never parallel: if $v_2 = c\,v_1$ then $Av_2 = \lambda_2 v_2 = \lambda_2 c\,v_1$, but also $Av_2 = c\,Av_1 = c\lambda_1 v_1$, so $\lambda_2 = \lambda_1$, which contradicts the eigenvalues being different. (For more than two eigenvalues a similar argument, adding one vector at a time, shows that eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are always linearly independent.) So $n$ different eigenvalues give $n$ independent eigenvectors.

A repeated eigenvalue may go either way. The identity matrix has $\lambda = 1$ twice and every vector is an eigenvector, so it is diagonalisable (it is already diagonal). The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 2$ twice, but $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ says $y = 0$, leaving only the line of $(1, 0)$. One eigenvector in a plane that needs two: the matrix is defective and cannot be diagonalised. Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues) explains this and what to do about it. A real matrix whose eigenvalues are complex but all different can still be diagonalised, with complex $P$ and $D$ (see Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues)), and a symmetric matrix always can, with perpendicular eigenvectors (see Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem (#/math/eigenvalues/symmetric-matrices)).
Similar matrices

Two matrices $A$ and $B$ are similar if $B = Q^{-1}AQ$ for some invertible $Q$: $B$ is the same linear map, described in a different basis. Diagonalisation says that a diagonalisable $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix. Similar matrices share their eigenvalues, because

since $Q^{-1}AQ - \lambda I = Q^{-1}(A - \lambda I)Q$ and $\det(Q^{-1})\det(Q) = 1$. So they also share trace and determinant. The eigenvectors change with the basis: if $Av = \lambda v$ then $B(Q^{-1}v) = Q^{-1}AQQ^{-1}v = \lambda\,Q^{-1}v$. A small example: with $Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, our $A$ becomes $B = Q^{-1}AQ = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$, a triangular matrix with eigenvalues 2 and 5 on its diagonal, as expected. The vector $v_1 = (1, 1)$ becomes $Q^{-1}v_1 = (0, 1)$, and indeed $B(0, 1) = (0, 5) = 5\,(0, 1)$.
Functions of a matrix

Once $A = PDP^{-1}$, any polynomial or power series in $A$ works the same way: $p(A) = P\,p(D)\,P^{-1}$, where $p(D)$ applies $p$ to each diagonal entry. So does the inverse, when no eigenvalue is zero: $A^{-1} = PD^{-1}P^{-1}$ with $D^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(\tfrac15, \tfrac12)$, which gives $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.3 & -0.1 \\ -0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$ (check: its top row times the first column of $A$ is $0.3 \cdot 4 - 0.1 \cdot 2 = 1$). The exponential, which solves the equation $x' = Ax$, is $e^{At} = P\,\operatorname{diag}(e^{5t}, e^{2t})\,P^{-1}$: at $t = 0$ this is $PP^{-1} = I$, and for large $t$ it is dominated by $e^{5t}$. Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications) takes this to differential equations and stability.
Practice

blocks.title: Diagonalise and take a power
blocks.text: Diagonalise $S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and find $S^5$.
solution: Eigenvalues 3 and 1 with vectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$. So $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(3, 1)$, and $P^{-1} = \tfrac12 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ (determinant $-2$).

$S^5 = P\,\operatorname{diag}(3^5, 1)\,P^{-1}$ with $3^5 = 243$. First $P D^5 = \begin{pmatrix} 243 & 1 \\ 243 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, then times $P^{-1}$: $\tfrac12 \begin{pmatrix} 243 + 1 & 243 - 1 \\ 243 - 1 & 243 + 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 122 & 121 \\ 121 & 122 \end{pmatrix}$.
Check: the entries of $S^5$ must sum along a row to $3^5 = 243$ (since $(1, 1)$ has eigenvalue 3): $122 + 121 = 243$.

blocks.title: Fibonacci by formula
blocks.text: Use Binet's formula to find $F_{20}$, and say how large the correction $\psi^{20}/\sqrt5$ is.
solution: $\varphi^{20} = 15\,126.99993$ and $\psi^{20} = 0.0000661$. So $F_{20} = (15\,126.99993 - 0.00007)/2.236068 = 6765$. The correction $\psi^{20}/\sqrt5$ is about $3 \times 10^{-5}$, far below the 0.5 needed to change the nearest whole number, so $F_{20}$ is the integer nearest to $\varphi^{20}/\sqrt5 = 6765.00003$.

blocks.title: Where does a Markov chain end up?
blocks.text: The matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ has columns that sum to 1. Show that $A(2, 1) = (2, 1)$ and $A(1, -1) = 0.7\,(1, -1)$, then find the limit of $A^k$ as $k \to \infty$.
solution: As $k \to \infty$, $0.7^k \to 0$, so $A^k \to P\,\operatorname{diag}(1, 0)\,P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac13 \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Every column of the limit is $(2/3, 1/3)$, the eigenvector with $\lambda = 1$ scaled to sum 1. Numerically $A^{60}$ already agrees to eight places.

blocks.title: Can it be diagonalised?
blocks.text: Is $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ diagonalisable? What about $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$?
solution: The first has $\lambda = 3$ twice, and $A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ forces $y = 0$: one eigen-direction. Not diagonalisable. The second is already diagonal. The third has the distinct eigenvalues 3 and 2 (the triangular diagonal), so it is diagonalisable. Its eigenvectors are $(1, 0)$ for $\lambda = 3$ and, from $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, which says $x + y = 0$, the vector $(1, -1)$ for $\lambda = 2$. Check: the matrix sends $(1, -1)$ to $(3 - 1,\ -2) = (2, -2) = 2\,(1, -1)$.
